name: Swift Bunny
toolCategory: Multifamily employee engagement and resident feedback platform

verdict.line: The only vendor in this set that is multifamily-native on both the employee and resident side — compete strictly on benchmark scale, CRE tenant coverage and the ability to route a finding into training, policy and mystery shop verification, never on their industry credibility.

founded.value: Launched publicly June 2019 at NAA Apartmentalize

ownership.value: Private. Founded by Joe Bailey (founder and former CEO/President of Grace Hill); Doug Miller (founder of SatisFacts Research and ManagInc) is Chief Research Officer and partner; Jen Piccotti is President. No outside ownership or investment publicly disclosed as of Aug 2026.

pricing.value: Not published. Site directs to a demo request; no pricing page or per-unit rate disclosed.

positioning.value: "Swift Bunny ONE" is positioned as an all-in-one employee retention platform for multifamily operators, built around Introduce (onboarding), Ingage (employee lifecycle feedback), Inquire (custom surveys) and Intouch (resident feedback), plus consultation and action planning.

strengths.text: Multifamily-native by design — the product is built only for rental housing operators, not adapted from a horizontal HR or survey tool.
Founding team carries deep multifamily lineage: Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill, and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts Research and ManagInc.

Covers both sides of the listening problem in one platform — Ingage for employee lifecycle feedback, Intouch for prospect and resident feedback — and explicitly links employee engagement to resident satisfaction.
Event-triggered lifecycle design on both sides: employee surveys fire at key moments in the employee lifecycle, resident/prospect feedback is solicited at key moments in the customer journey.
Intouch applies a proprietary algorithm across survey topic scores, importance and correlation with likelihood to renew to flag at-risk residents.
Publishes an annual Employee Engagement Risk Report and Employee Choice Awards, giving them recurring industry visibility.

gaps.text: Benchmark scale and history are not fully disclosed publicly. The Intouch page promises comparison to "rental housing peers" but discloses no respondent count, company count or years of history; the only public figure found is "over 6,500 multifamily employees nationwide last year" in the 2022 Employee Engagement Risk Report.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published product line, which lists Introduce, Ingage, Inquire and Intouch only.
No pricing is published on the site — buyers cannot self-serve a cost comparison.

The published product line covers feedback, onboarding and action planning; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product, so a finding cannot be routed to verified remediation inside the same platform.

whyWeWin: Benchmark depth: the Kingsley Index carries decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history; Swift Bunny does not publicly disclose comparable scale or history for its peer comparison.
CRE tenant coverage: Grace Hill surveys multifamily residents, employees and commercial tenants; Swift Bunny's published line is multifamily resident and employee only.

Closed loop: a Grace Hill survey finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the behavior actually changed — Swift Bunny stops at insight and action planning.
One vendor, one contract across surveys, training, policy and shopping instead of stacking a feedback point solution on top of an LMS.
askThis: When your Swift Bunny report shows a peer comparison, how many responses and how many companies is that comparison built from, and over how many years?
Do you need to benchmark commercial tenants as well as residents? How does that work today?
When a survey surfaces a fair housing or service issue at one property, what happens next — who assigns the training, and how do you confirm the behavior actually changed?
Are you running a separate LMS and a separate policy system alongside this? What does that cost you in admin time and reconciliation?

objections.objection: Swift Bunny was built by people who actually know multifamily.
objections.response: Agreed, and we say so openly — Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts. That is exactly why the comparison should be on scale and scope: the Kingsley Index brings decades of multifamily and CRE benchmarking history, and we can take a finding all the way through training, policy and a verification shop.

objections.objection: They do employee and resident feedback in one platform, same as you.
objections.response: They do — plus we add commercial tenant surveys, the Kingsley benchmark set, and the remediation path. Ask what happens on their side after the insight lands.

objections.objection: Their lifecycle triggers are more granular than an annual survey.
objections.response: Lifecycle and event-triggered surveys are table stakes for us too. The differentiator is what the number is compared against and what you can do about it inside the same system.

doNotSay: Never attack the industry credibility or multifamily experience of Swift Bunny's founders. Joe Bailey founded Grace Hill and Doug Miller founded SatisFacts Research — both facts are public and easily verified, and any 'they don't know multifamily' line will be disproven in the room and will cost you the deal. Compete only on benchmark scale, CRE tenant coverage and platform breadth.

Do not say 'Swift Bunny has no benchmark.' They publicly state Intouch compares a portfolio to rental housing peers. The accurate, defensible statement is that they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of that benchmark.
Do not say they are a startup or unproven — they have been shipping since 2019 and publish annual industry research.
Do not quote a Swift Bunny price, headcount, client count or benchmark size. None of these are publicly disclosed.
Do not claim they cannot do employee surveys well — employee lifecycle feedback is their founding product.
Do not imply any Grace Hill relationship, endorsement or shared data because of the founder history. There is none.

name: J Turner Research
toolCategory: Multifamily resident feedback and online reputation research

verdict.line: The reputation-score brand of multifamily — strong on reviews and ORA, but they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of their survey benchmark, and there is no training, policy or shop to close the loop.

founded.value: 2003, co-founded by Joseph Batdorf and Nitin Agarwal

ownership.value: Privately held. No acquisition, private equity investment or outside ownership publicly disclosed as of Aug 2026; company pages describe the two founders only.

size.value: 37 team members across 10 states (per company Our Story page)

pricing.value: Not published as a rate card. The site references a pricing page but discloses no rates.

positioning.value: "The Only Multifamily Specific, All-In-One Platform Designed to Improve Resident Experience" — surveys, review management, AI-assisted review and survey response, social media management, business listings and ORA monitoring.

strengths.text: The ORA (Online Reputation Assessment) score is an established, widely recognized multifamily standard — a 0-100 score aggregated across 20+ major review sites and ILSs, updated monthly, evaluating feedback across 22 operational areas.
Publishes monthly ORA Power Rankings and year-end summaries that rank properties and management companies, generating durable industry mindshare.
Broad survey line beyond the annual resident survey: resident, prospect, employee, student housing (Spring, Fall, Guarantor, Prospect) and custom surveys in Do-It-Yourself and Made-to-Order formats.
Action Planning Tool (APT) lets teams create and execute S.M.A.R.T. goals against high-priority feedback, and PUSH for Reviews converts survey respondents into public reviewers.
Einstein, their AI tool, is described as having analyzed over 12 million reviews.
Bundles adjacent reputation services — review response, social media management and business listings — into the same platform.
Sells surveys and reputation together to the same multifamily buyer, in one vendor relationship.
ORA is a published, named multifamily reputation metric with a competitor-monitoring product wrapped around it ("intelligence into your high-priority competition").
Response Solutions are marketed as "Review & Survey Response — Powered by AI and Expert Guidance," i.e. a human-supervised managed offering rather than tooling alone.
Business listings management covers "hundreds of business listings for your communities."

gaps.text: Survey benchmark scale and history are not publicly disclosed. Neither the ORA FAQ nor the surveys solution page states the number of survey respondents, the number of participating companies, or the number of years of survey history. The 12-million figure is reviews analyzed by the Einstein AI tool, not survey benchmark scale.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published survey line, which covers resident, prospect, employee, student housing and custom surveys.

The published platform is surveys plus reputation; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product, so a finding cannot be routed to verified remediation in the same system.
No pricing is published.
No training, policy or mystery-shopping line is offered — the solutions page lists surveys, reviews, response, social, listings, ORA monitoring and support only.
Tier pricing is not published; the pricing page names Smart / Smarter / Smartest / Genius tiers but shows no per-tier price.
Review generation / solicitation is not described on the solutions page as a named capability.

whyWeWin: Benchmark provenance: the Kingsley Index publishes decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history; J Turner does not publicly state the scale or history behind its survey comparisons.
CRE tenant surveys: Grace Hill covers commercial tenants alongside residents and employees; J Turner's published survey line does not.

Closed loop: our survey finding assigns training, updates the policy, and a mystery shop verifies the behavior changed — a reputation score tells you the number moved but not why or whether the fix stuck.
A reputation score is an outcome metric. Structured survey data plus benchmarks tells you which operational driver to fix first.

Reputation sits inside PerformanceHQ next to training, policy, surveys and shopping — a recurring review theme can route to a course assignment or a policy acknowledgment without leaving the platform.
Grace Hill can act on the finding, not just report it; a research firm hands you the number and stops.
One vendor for the whole people-and-performance stack reduces the number of integrations and contracts the operator carries.
askThis: When you see your ORA score move, what tells you which operational driver caused it?
How many survey responses and how many companies is your benchmark comparison built from, and over what period?
Do you need to benchmark commercial tenants too? How is that handled today?
Once a survey flags a service or fair housing issue at a property, who assigns the training and how do you verify it took?
Are you paying separately for surveys, review response, social and listings? What does the all-in number look like?
When ORA flags a property, what actually happens on site the next week — who owns the fix?
Are your survey vendor and your review-response vendor the same team, and do their reports reconcile?
Which of your review responses are written by a person and which by a model — and who reviews the fair housing language before it posts?
How is ORA calculated for a property with low review volume, and how do you handle a property that just opened?

objections.objection: ORA is the industry standard — everyone benchmarks on it.
objections.response: ORA is a genuinely well-known reputation score and we don't argue with that. It measures what the public says about you. Our benchmark measures what your residents, employees and commercial tenants tell you directly, against decades of Kingsley data — and then routes the finding into training and a verification shop.

objections.objection: They cover reviews, social and listings in one place.
objections.response: They do, and that's real breadth on the reputation side. The question is what happens after a problem is identified — that's where a training, policy and mystery shop stack changes the outcome rather than the score.

objections.objection: They're multifamily-specific like you are.
objections.response: Agreed. So the comparison narrows to benchmark depth, commercial tenant coverage, and whether a finding can be closed inside the platform.

objections.objection: Our owners already look at ORA.
objections.response: Then keep watching it. The question is what changes the score. Ask them who assigns the training and policy work that moves maintenance and communication themes — that is where PerformanceHQ plugs in.

objections.objection: They're multifamily specialists, you're a platform company.
objections.response: Grace Hill has been multifamily-only for decades across training, policy, surveys and shopping. The specialization argument runs both ways — ours spans the operating problem, not just the measurement.

doNotSay: Do not claim J Turner's data is biased, inflated or compromised. There is no public basis for it and it is a liability statement.
Do not say 'they have no benchmark' — they publish ORA Power Rankings and comparative scoring. Say instead that they do not publicly disclose the scale or history of their survey benchmark.
Do not present the '12 million reviews' figure as survey respondents. It is reviews analyzed by their Einstein AI tool.
Do not quote a J Turner price, client count or revenue figure — none are published.
Do not state that J Turner has been acquired or is PE-owned. No such disclosure was found; if a rep hears otherwise, verify before repeating.
Do not characterize ORA's methodology or claim it is inaccurate — the calculation is theirs and publicly described.
Avoid 'the only platform that connects reputation to training' — a buyer with a browser will find other bundles. State our workflow specifically instead.

name: SatisFacts & ApartmentRatings
toolCategory: Multifamily resident survey and online reputation platform

verdict.line: Deep multifamily survey line paired with the ApartmentRatings review site under Internet Brands — compete on benchmark disclosure, commercial tenant coverage and the ability to close the loop into training and mystery shopping.

hq.value: Unknown — not disclosed on the SatisFacts site; parent Internet Brands is headquartered in El Segundo, CA

founded.value: SatisFacts Research founded by Doug Miller (per Swift Bunny launch release, which describes him as "the founder of SatisFacts Research"); exact founding year not disclosed on the SatisFacts site

ownership.value: Owned by MH Sub I, LLC dba Internet Brands. Internet Brands (owner of ApartmentRatings.com) acquired SatisFacts Research in July 2012 and combined the two.

pricing.value: Not published. No rates disclosed on the products or homepage.

positioning.value: "The leading provider of resident surveys focusing on multifamily retention and reputation management" — an integrated survey plus reputation stack sold under the joint SatisFacts & ApartmentRatings brand, anchored by the epIQ Index.

strengths.text: Broad multifamily survey line: Annual resident satisfaction survey, Insite event-triggered feedback surveys, FLEX customizable surveys, Takeover surveys for pre-acquisition assessment, and an Employee Feedback Survey.

The epIQ Index (Experience & Performance Intelligence Quotient) is positioned as a single letter-grade performance metric combining verified ApartmentRatings and SatisFacts data across four variables on a rolling 365-day period, updated daily.
Owns distribution: ApartmentRatings.com profiles more than 150,000 communities across the U.S., giving SatisFacts a review-site footprint most survey vendors do not have.
Explicitly ties employee engagement to resident outcomes, positioning the employee survey to show "how your employees' level of engagement directly impacts resident loyalty and revenue growth."

Full reputation stack alongside surveys: Verified Review Program, Review Responder (claimed "5.5x faster" responses), Reputation Management across 100+ sites, Google Direct, and the LEO all-in-one bundle.

Runs a national awards program with published, specific eligibility thresholds — 2024 winners required a minimum of 100 (management company) or 25 (community) Insite or Annual survey completions and a portfolio score of 4.25 or above out of 5.0; 3,445 communities nationwide qualified.
Review Responder is a managed service: responses are "crafted by industry experts — all within 24 business hours."
Broad multifamily survey line — Annual Resident Satisfaction, Insite touchpoint, Employee, FLEX and Takeover (due-diligence) surveys.
Structural tie to ApartmentRatings and the epIQ Index report card, a review property multifamily owners already track.
Verified Review Program and Google Direct give solicited reviews a route onto sites that matter to leasing.

gaps.text: Survey benchmark scale and history are not disclosed. Neither the homepage, products page nor the epIQ Index page states total survey respondents, number of participating companies, or years of survey history; the only history claim found is "over 10 years of historical data" attached to their biennial Online Renter Study, not the survey benchmark.
No commercial real estate tenant survey product appears in the published product line, which is multifamily resident and employee only.

The epIQ Index is composed of review ratings, review count per unit, manager review engagement rate and manager reply time — three of the four inputs measure review-response behavior rather than operational service quality.
The published product line covers surveys and reputation; it does not list a training/LMS, policy management or mystery shopping product.
No pricing is published.
No training, policy management or mystery-shopping line — the product suite is surveys plus reputation only.
No pricing is published anywhere on the site.
Competitor benchmarking is not described as a product capability on the site's solution pages.

whyWeWin: Benchmark disclosure and depth: the Kingsley Index publishes decades of multifamily and CRE benchmarking history; SatisFacts does not publicly disclose the scale or history behind its survey comparisons.
CRE tenant surveys: Grace Hill covers commercial tenants; the SatisFacts line does not.
Closed loop: a survey finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the change — SatisFacts stops at survey and review response.
Independence: our benchmark and our reporting are not tied to a consumer review property, so there is no question about how the two interact.
PerformanceHQ turns a review theme into an assignment — training, policy acknowledgment or a shop — inside the same platform the survey data lives in.
Grace Hill's survey benchmark and reputation view sit in the same reporting layer as workforce data, so a regional manager sees cause and effect on one screen.
Our reputation offering is not tied to a review site we also operate, which removes a conflict-of-interest question some owners raise.
askThis: Your survey vendor and the public review site are the same company. How do you think about that when you're reading your own score?
How many survey responses and how many companies sit behind the benchmark you're compared to, and over how many years?
Three of the four epIQ inputs relate to reviews and how fast managers reply. How do you separate 'we respond quickly' from 'the service is actually good'?
Do you need commercial tenant surveys as well? Where does that live today?
When a survey flags an issue at a property, who assigns the training, and how do you verify the behavior changed?
Who owns your epIQ score internally, and what do they do with it in a given month?
When your survey vendor and your review vendor are the same company, how do you separate what residents told you privately from what they posted publicly?
How long does a response actually take to appear on Google after a one-star review lands on a Friday?
What happens to a recurring maintenance complaint after it shows up in both the survey and the reviews?

objections.objection: SatisFacts has been doing multifamily resident surveys longer than almost anyone.
objections.response: True, and their survey line is genuinely deep. The comparison is on benchmark transparency, whether commercial tenants are in scope, and what happens after the finding lands.

objections.objection: We get surveys and our ApartmentRatings presence from one vendor.
objections.response: That's a real convenience. It's also worth asking how you'd read your own numbers if the benchmark and the public review site sat with two independent parties.

objections.objection: epIQ gives us one score to manage to.
objections.response: It's a clean number. Just note what it's made of — review ratings, review volume per unit, manager response rate and reply time. Faster replies move it. Fixing the underlying service issue is a different exercise, and that's where training, policy and a verification shop come in.

objections.objection: They already own ApartmentRatings, so their data is better.
objections.response: It is one source among many. Ask what share of your prospect traffic comes from ApartmentRatings versus Google, and whether your reputation strategy should be organized around a single site's index.

objections.objection: We already use SatisFacts for surveys, adding response is easy.
objections.response: It is easy — and it stops at the reply. Ask what happens after the reply: who is assigned what, and where is the proof the number moved.

doNotSay: Never assert that SatisFacts or ApartmentRatings data is biased, manipulated or compromised because the survey vendor and review site share an owner. There is no public evidence for it, it is defamatory in tone, and it is a legal risk. Ask the neutral question instead — it is in askThis.

Do not claim the 150,000+ figure is survey respondents. It is the number of communities profiled on ApartmentRatings.com.
Do not attribute Internet Brands corporate facts (revenue, headcount, other properties) to SatisFacts.
Do not quote a SatisFacts price or client count — none are published.

Do not claim SatisFacts manipulates ApartmentRatings ratings — there is no public source for that and it is legally risky.
Do not say they 'have no benchmarking' — say it is not described on their public product pages.

verdict.line: The cheap, familiar way to send a survey — it gives you a distribution mechanism and a generic benchmark, not a multifamily peer comparison or anyone accountable for what the answer means.

founded.value: 1999, by Ryan Finley (later joined by Chris Finley)

ownership.value: Private. Rebranded to Momentive Global in June 2021; a Zendesk acquisition was rejected by shareholders in 2021; acquired by a Symphony Technology Group-led consortium for $1.5 billion, completed May 2023, after which the company reverted to the SurveyMonkey brand.

strengths.text: Published, self-serve pricing — a buyer can price it without a sales call: Team Advantage $30/user/month, Team Premier $92/user/month, billed annually.
Enormous familiarity and reach: over 250,000 organizations and 42 million users, supported in 56+ languages across 190+ countries.

Benchmark data is limited to select Question Bank questions and is available in English only.
No multifamily or commercial real estate benchmark is offered; benchmarks are generic industry cuts on standardized questions.
No resident, CRE tenant or property-portfolio survey product exists — the product is a general-purpose survey builder, so question design, rollup logic and analysis are the customer's responsibility.
Priced per user per month, so cost scales with the number of people who need to build or read surveys rather than with portfolio size.

whyWeWin: A tool sends the survey; a program tells you what the number means. Kingsley gives the multifamily and CRE peer comparison SurveyMonkey structurally cannot.
Property, region and portfolio rollups arrive built; in SurveyMonkey somebody on your team builds and maintains them.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one benchmarked program instead of three disconnected survey files.
The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update and a mystery shop that verifies the fix.

Their benchmarks cover select Question Bank questions in English only. Does your resident base need Spanish?

What happens between a bad survey result and someone actually changing behavior at the property?

objections.objection: They have benchmarks too.

strengths.text: Well-defined niche with disclosed traction: 350,000+ renter conversations, 65,000 move-ins and 1,500+ communities served.

whyWeWin: Not applicable as a head-to-head — Rentgrata and Grace Hill Surveys solve different problems and can coexist in the same account.

name: Status Quo — DIY surveys or no formal listening program
toolCategory: In-house survey effort using a free tool, a spreadsheet, or no formal listening program at all

verdict.line: The most common competitor in the set and the hardest to dislodge — never mock it, credit what it genuinely gets right, then compete on the one thing it structurally cannot produce: a comparison to peer operators.

pricing.value: Effectively free in hard dollars — a free survey tool, an existing spreadsheet, or nothing at all. The real cost is staff time, which is rarely tracked.

positioning.value: "We already know what our residents think — our managers talk to them every day, we read every review, and we send a survey once a year."

strengths.text: It costs nothing in hard dollars and requires no procurement, no security review and no new contract — a real advantage when budgets are tight.
The questions are exactly the questions leadership wants answered, with no vendor's standard instrument in the way.
Nobody has to learn a new system, and there is no implementation project competing for onsite attention.

Experienced operators genuinely do know a great deal about their properties. A good regional manager walking a site picks up things no survey captures, and dismissing that instinct is the fastest way to lose the room.
Reading reviews is free, immediate and unfiltered — it is real feedback, and operators who do it consistently do catch problems.
Zero vendor risk: no renewal, no price increase, no dependency on someone else's roadmap.

gaps.text: No external comparison. A score of 78 with no peer set cannot tell an operator whether they are winning or losing — this is a structural property of any in-house instrument, not a claim about a specific vendor.

Reviews are a self-selected sample. Residents who post are disproportionately those with a strong grievance or a strong attachment; the quiet majority whose renewal decision is actually in play is largely absent.
An annual survey surfaces a problem up to twelve months after it started, by which point the affected residents have already made renewal decisions.
Question wording usually drifts year over year in a DIY instrument, which quietly destroys the ability to trend results reliably.
Response rates are typically not managed — no reminder cadence, no channel testing, no non-response analysis — so results skew toward whoever happened to open the email.
Employee feedback is usually absent entirely, so an operator cannot see the link between team engagement and resident outcomes.
Commercial tenants, where a portfolio has them, are almost never surveyed under a DIY program.
Results live in a spreadsheet with no property, region or portfolio rollup, so the executive view has to be rebuilt by hand each cycle.
Nothing connects a finding to remediation: no assigned training, no policy update, no verification that the behavior changed.
The program depends on one person. When that analyst or marketing coordinator leaves, the survey usually stops.
The staff time cost is real but invisible, because it is never priced against the free tool it replaces.

whyWeWin: The Kingsley Index answers the one question no in-house survey can: is a 78 good for a portfolio like yours?
Decades of multifamily and commercial real estate benchmarking history means the comparison holds up in an investor conversation, not just an internal one.
Residents, employees and commercial tenants in one benchmarked program instead of three disconnected efforts.
A consistent instrument means year-over-year trending actually works.
Continuous, event-triggered listening finds the problem in the week it happens instead of at the next annual cycle.
The finding routes into assigned training, a policy update, and a mystery shop that verifies the behavior changed — the DIY path ends at the chart.
askThis: When your survey comes back at 78, how do you know whether that's good?
How would you explain that number to an investor or a lender who asked how you compare to peer operators?
Who owns running the survey today, and what happens to the program if that person leaves?
Did the questions change between last year's survey and this year's? Can you still trend it?
What was your response rate, and do you know how the people who didn't answer differ from the people who did?
Are you measuring your onsite teams as well as your residents? Can you tell whether turnover at a property is driving the resident scores?
When last year's survey flagged a maintenance issue at three properties, what happened next — and how did you confirm it got fixed?
Roughly how many hours did the last survey cycle take across your team, start to finish?

objections.objection: We already do our own survey and it works fine.
objections.response: That's genuinely more than a lot of operators do, and it means you already believe in listening. The one thing it can't give you is context — a 78 with no peer set doesn't tell you whether to celebrate or act. That's what the benchmark adds.

objections.objection: Our managers already know what residents think.
objections.response: Many of them do, and the good ones are usually right. The problem is you can't roll up instinct across 40 properties, defend it to an investor, or trend it year over year. The survey doesn't replace their judgment — it makes it comparable.

objections.objection: We read every review, that's our feedback loop.
objections.response: Reviews are real feedback and worth reading. They're also self-selected — you hear from the delighted and the furious. The residents whose renewal is genuinely undecided rarely post, and those are the ones the number depends on.

objections.objection: We don't have budget for this.
objections.response: Fair. Worth pricing the current approach honestly, though — the hours to build, send, chase, clean and roll up the survey, plus the cost of finding out about a problem eleven months late.

objections.objection: We'd rather build it ourselves in a tool we already have.
objections.response: You can build the instrument. What you can't build is the peer comparison set, and you'll own question design, response-rate management and rollup logic permanently.

doNotSay: Never mock or belittle the buyer's current approach. They built it, they may have defended it internally, and insulting it makes the decision personal.
Do not claim the buyer 'has no idea' what residents think. Many experienced operators have accurate instincts, and telling them otherwise ends the conversation.
Do not invent a statistic about what DIY surveys cost, what response rates they achieve, or how much revenue poor listening loses. If you need a number, ask the buyer for theirs.
Do not cite an industry study, retention percentage or ROI figure unless it is a Grace Hill-approved, sourced claim.
Do not claim reviews are worthless — they are useful and free, just self-selected.
Do not promise a specific score improvement, retention lift or NOI impact from switching.

sv-benchmark-dataset.note: There is no external comparison set. This is the defining structural limitation of the status quo.

sv-benchmark-scale.note: No benchmark exists, so no scale or history can be disclosed. The buyer's own historical data is the only comparison available, and only if question wording stayed consistent.

sv-portfolio-rollup.note: Rollups are rebuilt by hand in a spreadsheet each cycle, if at all.

sv-lifecycle.note: Typically a single annual send; event-triggered lifecycle surveys require automation the status quo does not have.

sv-custom-questions.note: Full control over questions is the status quo's genuine strength — though without a benchmarked core, the answers have nothing to be compared against.

sv-sentiment.note: Open-text responses are read manually, if at all.

sv-investor-grade.note: An unbenchmarked internal score does not stand up in an investor or lender conversation.

sv-action-planning.note: No structured action planning; follow-up depends on whoever reads the spreadsheet.

sv-published-pricing.note: Free or near-free in hard dollars — the staff time cost is real but untracked.
